answer.rationale:
The binding constraint is that the contract expires in 14 days with the line at 94% of committed volume and no buffer. That eliminates switch_primary_vendor as a first move this cycle: memory_c2 reports a fast, clean cutover, but it says nothing about doing so under a two-week deadline with zero slack, and a cost win that stops the line fails the stated objective (cost down WITHOUT added delivery risk). add_second_source (memory_c3) is attractive on resilience but does not by itself secure primary supply past day 85, so it leaves the real exposure untouched. renew_incumbent (memory_c1) is safe on delivery and simply concedes the 18% mandate. defer_decision (memory_c5) worked on a NON-critical service on month-to-month terms; this is the critical primary contract with no evidence of a month-to-month fallback, so that precedent does not transfer.

That leaves negotiate_terms as the only lever that touches both cost and continuity. The incumbent refused to reopen PRICE this cycle, which is a narrower refusal than it looks: memory_c6 says multi-year term commitment unlocked volume pricing, and memory_c4 says market benchmarking moved both price and payment terms. Those are different instruments than a mid-cycle price reopen, so the refusal does not obviously foreclose them.

I am spending the single verification on memory_c6 because it is the load-bearing claim for my chosen action and the one I am least able to check by inference. I need to know whether the volume pricing came from term length itself or from a volume tier Halden can no longer credibly promise at 94% utilization with a finance-mandated 18% spend cut - a shrinking spend envelope may disqualify us from the very tier that made c6 work. I also want to see whether c6's 'service scope did not narrow' held over the full term or only at signing. I did not verify memory_c2 because even a fully confirmed c2 would not change this cycle's action given the 14-day clock.

Scope: keep this a small guarded move - a short bridge extension or near-term floor that secures supply past day 85, with any multi-year structure carrying exit rights and no volume floor above current committed volume.

Residual uncertainty I am not resolving: whether negotiation yields anywhere near 18% (it may yield 5-8%, leaving a gap to close next cycle), and whether the incumbent's refusal is a genuine floor or an opening position. Downstream risk to flag explicitly: a multi-year lock-in deepens single-source dependency exactly where memory_c3 warns about a single point of failure, and it forecloses the memory_c2 cost path for the term's duration. It also risks meeting the 18% number by quietly narrowing scope - c6 claims that did not happen, which is precisely what verification should confirm. I would sequence add_second_source as the next cycle's decision and cap any term at the shortest length that clears the pricing tier.
